cues.text: In 1517, a priest in Salzano, near Venice in Italy, received word that a parishioner lay dying and needed to receive the Viaticum — Communion given to those near death.
Because of the late hour and the season, there was no time to organize the usual solemn procession.
The priest set out with only a single altar boy for company, carrying the Blessed Sacrament across the meadows bordering the Muson River.
As the small party crossed the fields, several donkeys grazing nearby turned to face the approaching priest.
Drawing near, they bent their knees before the Blessed Sacrament he carried—a gesture of recognition the animals had no evident reason to make of their own accord.
Having genuflected, the donkeys fell in alongside the small procession and followed it all the way to the dying parishioner's house.
There, they renewed their genuflection before accompanying the priest back across the same fields toward their own pasture.
Finally, they returned to grazing as though nothing unusual had happened.
In memory of the event, the Cathedral of San Bartolomeo in Salzano still preserves an altar cloth linked by long tradition to the miracle, kept and venerated by the parish community.
Ignatius of Loyola and his early companions are said to have passed through the region only a couple of decades later, in 1536.
They drew the attention of a wider Catholic reform movement already gathering in nearby Venice to a devotion still fresh in local memory.
The Salzano account belongs to a distinct and gentler category among Eucharistic traditions: no theft, no violence, and no doubt to be resolved.
Only ordinary animals, in the telling, recognized what the faithful believed they carried past them in the field.

It remains one of the more widely retold Eucharistic accounts precisely for that simplicity, offered still today as evidence, however one weighs it, that reverence for the Sacrament was not confined to those capable of understanding what it was.
